body.p: Claims 1-18 are pending in this Office Action. By this communication, claims 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 and 17 are amended, and claim 2, 8 and 14 are cancelled. Applicant thanks the Examiner for carefully considering this application. Claim Amendments

Independent claim 1 is amended by incorporating features of claim 2 which is cancelled accordingly. Independent claim 1 is amended by including "implemented by an autonomous driving system of a vehicle" and "performing lane changing of the vehicle based on the lane changing preparation pose." Support for the amendment can be found at least in page 3, line 15, page 6, line 12-13, of the specification as originally filed.

The similar amendment is made on independent claims 7 and 13. Accordingly, claims 8 and 14 are cancelled without prejudice or disclaimer. No new matter is added by any amendment made herein. Entry and favorable consideration thereof is respectfully requested. Claim Rejections - 35 U.S.C. § 101

Claim(s) 1-18 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to abstract idea without significantly more. (See MPEP § 2106.) Applicant respectfully traverses this rejection for at least the following reasons.

Applicant disagrees with the rationale set forth in the Office Action. Nevertheless, in the interest of expediting prosecution, Applicant has amended independent claim 1 to recite "A method for controlling lane changing, implemented by an autonomous driving system of a vehicle, comprising: predicting...; determining a lane changing preparation pose of the vehicle on the first

lane based on the target pose, a minimum turning radius of the vehicle and at least one safe distance parameter of the vehicle; performing lane changing of the vehicle based on the lane changing preparation pose". Independent claims 7 and 13 are similarly amended.

The Office contends that the present claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. Applicant respectfully submits that the additionally recited features of the amended claims negate the Office's reasoning. Thus, the amended claims do not fall within a judicial exception to subject matter eligibility. Furthermore, assuming, arguendo, that the claims do fall within a judicial exception, it is clearly integrated into a practical application of that exception and the claims recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Applicant's reasoning is provided in detail below.
As noted by the Examiner, the Office's 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance has been incorporated into MPEP §§ 2106.03-2106.07(c). The current evaluation procedure is as follows:

1. Step 1: Determine whether the claimed subject matter falls within the four statutory categories of patentable subject matter identified by 35 U.S.C 101: i.e., process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter;
2. Step 2(A)(i): Determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception, such as an abstract idea;
3. Step 2(A)(ii): Determine whether the recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application of that exception; and
4. Step 2(B): Determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
The Office does not contest that the claims fall within the four statutory categories of patentable subject matter.

The Examiner states that the claimed invention is directed to "an abstract idea which is directed to mental process" Office Action at page 3. Applicant respectfully disagrees and submits that the amended claim is clearly performed by an autonomous driving system of a vehicle, and therefore is not a "mathematical concept," a "method for organizing human activity," or a "mental process." In this regard, it should be borne in mind that an abstract idea may still be patentable if it is integrated into a practical application of that exception. In particular, Applicant respectfully notes that independent claims 1, 7 and 13, as currently amended, recite substantially more than the alleged abstract idea.

Based on the above, Applicant submits that the next inquiry should be to determine whether the claim recites a judicial exception such as an abstract idea. Section I of the Revised Eligibility Guidance sets forth three general classes of abstract ideas: mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.

Assuming, arguendo, that the claims recite an abstract idea of "mental process" (and apparatuses therefor) as alleged in the outstanding Office Action, Applicant respectfully submits that any such alleged abstract idea may still be patentable, provided that it is integrated into a practical application of that exception.
The next step of the evaluation calls for the Examiner to determine whether the recited judicial exception is integrated into a practical application of that exception.
According to the Revised Eligibility Guidance:

A claim is not "directed to" a judicial exception, and thus is patent eligible, if a claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.
Applicant respectfully submits that this step of the evaluation excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.

In the context of this step of the evaluation, it is indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) may have integrated the exception into a practical application, if an additional element reflects an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to
other technology or technical field.

The Federal Circuit has distinguished between claims that are "directed to" a judicial exception and those that are not. In McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco Games America Inc., 837 F.3d 1299 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("McRO"), the Court explained that under Alice Corp. "a court must look to the claims as an ordered combination, without ignoring the requirements of the individual steps." Page 21, paragraph 2.
The Court in McRO further stated that courts should ascertain whether the claims "focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology or are instead directed to

a result or effect that itself is an abstract idea." Page 23, paragraph 2. The Court found that the claims in that case were not generic, because they "are limited to rules with certain common characteristics" (page 22, paragraph 2), which resulted in an improvement in an existing technological process through the use of the claimed rules.

With the presently amended claims, it is respectfully submitted that the claims integrate the alleged abstract idea of lane changing with the use of unique elements to provide an improvement in the technological field of autonomous driving technologies. See, e.g., page 1, lines 10-11 of the originally filed specification. Additionally, the amended claim is provide for improving a success rate and safety of changing lanes for the vehicle. See, e.g., page 6, lines 14 of the originally filed specification. More particularly, the lane changing preparation pose fully considers the current pose, the target pose and the parameter of the vehicle, so that the vehicle is controlled to change lanes based on the lane changing preparation pose in a process of changing lanes, which is beneficial to improving a success rate and safety of changing lanes for the vehicle. Thus, the claims are eligible under this prong 2A because they are not directed to the alleged judicial exception.

In McRO, the Court stated that the claimed process was not the same as the previously performed manual process; therefore, the "claimed rules, not the use of the computer" were what "improved [the] existing technological process."

As discussed in the present specification, the method, apparatus, and non-transitory computer readable storage media of the present application improve the art by improving a success rate and safety of changing lanes for the vehicle.
The Court in McRO also stated that: "[t]he claimed process uses a combined order of specific rules that renders information into a specific format that is then used and applied to create
desired results" and "[w]hile the result may not be tangible, there is nothing that requires a method be tied to a machine or transform an article to be patentable."
It is clear from the present application that the claimed subject matter improves an existing technological process and not merely the use of a computer per se.

In Enfish, LLC v. Microsoft Corp., 822 F.3d 1327, 1334 (Fed. Cir. 2016) ("Enfish"), the Federal Circuit stated: "the first step in the Alice inquiry in this case asks whether the focus of the claims is on the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities (i.e., the self-referential table for a computer database) or, instead, on a process that qualifies as an "abstract idea" for which computers are invoked merely as a tool."

The Court accordingly held that: "[i]n other words, we are not faced with a situation where general-purpose computer components are added post-hoc to a fundamental economic practice or mathematical equation. Rather, the claims are directed to a specific implementation of a solution to a problem in the software arts. Accordingly, we find the claims at issue are not directed to an abstract idea." As indicated above, the presently claimed solution addresses problems in the technical field and is not merely an abstract idea.

Applicant accordingly submits that the present application is focused on a specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities, by performing operations that are not capable of reproduction by a human and is not merely an abstract idea wherein a computer is used as a tool.

Applicant also notes that, in claim 1 as amended, the alleged exception is integrated into a practical application and the newly added features constitute significantly more than the alleged exception. On this point, the recited method includes "determining a lane changing preparation pose of the vehicle on the first lane based on the target pose, a minimum turning radius of the vehicle and

at least one safe distance parameter of the vehicle; performing lane changing of the vehicle based on the lane changing preparation pose". These specific features are not well-understood, routine, or conventional in the field for at least the reasons discussed below in the traversal of the § 102 rejection. See MPEP 2106.05(1)(A)(v). Thus, the additional elements amount of an inventive concept.

However, even if the Examiner alleges that the invention is not patent-eligible according to Steps 2(A)(i) and 2(A)(ii), as per the Revised Eligibility Guidance, Applicant respectfully submits that the final stage of the evaluation (Step 2(B)) then has to be completed to determine whether the claimed invention is patent-eligible. Step 2(B)

The Examiner states that any additional elements recited are generic computer components performing functions similar to the computer functions described in Alice Corp. as being well-understood, routine and conventional.

This step of the evaluation calls for the Examiner to determine whether any element or combination of elements in the claim is sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. According to the Revised Eligibility Guidance: Therefore, if a claim has been determined to be directed to a judicial exception under revised Step 2(A), examiners should then evaluate the additional elements individually and in combination under Step 2(8) to determine whether they provide an inventive concept (i.e., whether the additional elements amount to significantly more than the exception itself).

However, when the examiner reconsiders the data gathering steps in Step 2(B), the examiner could determine that the combination of steps gather data in an unconventional way and therefore include an "inventive concept", rendering the claim eligible at Step 2B.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with Examiner's observations discussed above. The present claims are more specific and provide for the benefits discussed above and in the present specification. The generic utilization of known functions of a computer would not enable these improvements. Additionally, the claim features discussed more particularly below with respect to the § 102 rejection constitute an inventive concept and are not merely conventional.

Applicant therefore respectfully submits that the subject claims do involve an invention and ingenuity well beyond the generic utilization of the known functions of a program or operation of a computer, or implementation by a computer to operate the method. Withdrawal of the § 101 rejection is respectfully requested.

Claim(s) 1,7 and 13 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by US 20200241547 Al ("Hashimoto"). The rejections are respectfully traversed overcome by amendment in view of the following remarks.
As previously stated, Applicant amends independent claims 1, 7 and 13 to include allowable subject matter from dependent claims 2, 8 and 14, respectively. Therefore, amended claims
1, 7 and 13 are allowable. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1,
7 and 13 under 35 U.S.C. § 102 be reconsidered and withdrawn.

It is submitted that this Amendment has antecedent basis in the application as originally filed, including the specification, claims and drawings, and that this Amendment does not add any new subject matter to the application. It is submitted that this Amendment places the application in suitable condition for allowance, notice of which is requested. The Examiner is invited to contact the undersigned at the telephone number listed below if the Examiner believes an Examiner's amendment would expedite prosecution of the Application.
